in_context.text: This verse opens a short instruction to slaves in the church (6:1-2). It closes Paul's section on caring for different groups in the church: widows, elders, and servants. Right after it, the letter turns to false teachers and the love of money.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer in 1:1. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in his name. Others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: The letter is addressed to Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, who was leading the church at Ephesus. Timothy is told to "teach and exhort" these things to the church.

affected.text: Believers who were slaves ("under the yoke"), and their masters. Verse 2 turns to slaves whose masters were also believers.

what.text: Slaves in the church are told to regard their own masters as worthy of full respect. The stated reason is so that God's name and the Christian teaching would not be spoken against.

events.text: The instruction applies to the church at Ephesus while Timothy led it, under the emperor Nero (AD 54-68).

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: The letter was sent to Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Where it was written from is not stated, though it may have been Macedonia.

purpose.text: The concern is the church's reputation. Paul wants believers' behavior to keep outsiders from speaking against God and his teaching. Titus 2:5 and Romans 2:24 voice the same worry.

big_picture.text: A key theme of the letter is that sound teaching and godly living belong together. How believers act in ordinary roles either honors or shames the message.

for_readers.text: The verse asks believers to consider how their conduct reflects on God's name. Elsewhere Paul tells a slave who can gain freedom to take it. He also says that in the Lord a slave is "the Lord's freeman."

misuse.popular_reading: Quoted as if God approves of slavery as an institution, or as a blanket rule that people must submit to any master or boss without question.

in_context_reading.text: The verse speaks to slaves already living under that system and urges conduct that would not bring shame on God's name. It does not argue that slavery is good. Paul elsewhere urges slaves who can become free to take it (1 Cor 7:21).

why_it_matters.text: The KJV says "servants," but the Greek word means a slave, a person in bondage. The verse is about slaves, not hired workers.
The yoke is used as a picture of bondage or submission to authority. This makes clear the people addressed were not free.
This word for master implied absolute ownership and unchecked power. That shows how hard the slaves' situation was.
The word means to speak profanely or insultingly of sacred things. The verse's goal is to keep outsiders from speaking against God because of believers' conduct.

takeaway.text: This verse tells believing slaves to respect their masters for the sake of God's reputation. It is not an endorsement of slavery. Its point is that Christians' everyday conduct reflects on God's name.

unsupported.reason: The lexicon only cites Thayer contrasting δεσπότης with κύριος as denoting absolute ownership. The added conclusion that this 'shows how hard the slaves' situation was' goes beyond the source.
